note:
A 10-year-old male was seen in the otolaryngology clinic with his mother for evaluation of recurrent tonsillitis. Over the past 12 months he has had five episodes of sore throat with fever, each treated by his pediatrician with a 10-day course of amoxicillin, the most recent about 3 weeks ago. Between episodes he feels well and eats normally. His mother reports that he misses several school days with each episode and snores mildly at night. He denies ear pain, hearing difficulty, and breathing difficulty during the day. He has no known drug allergies and takes no daily medications.

On examination he is afebrile with a temperature of 98.4 F and a heart rate of 84. The tonsils are 3+ and symmetric with cryptic debris and no exudate today. There is no erythema of the posterior pharynx. Tender anterior cervical lymph nodes of about 1 cm are palpable bilaterally. Tympanic membranes are clear. As part of the combined eye screening, visual acuity is 20/20 in each eye and there is no conjunctival injection or discharge.

My impression is recurrent tonsillitis with tonsillar hypertrophy. With five documented episodes in one year, he meets criteria for surgical evaluation. I discussed the risks and benefits of tonsillectomy with his mother, who would like to proceed. I am referring him for tonsillectomy and have asked her to give ibuprofen 200 mg every 6 hours as needed for throat pain until surgery. We will see him back in clinic in 4 weeks before the operation, and she will call sooner for high fever or trouble swallowing.
summary: A 10-year-old male was seen in the otolaryngology clinic with his mother for recurrent tonsillitis, with five episodes of sore throat and fever in the past 12 months, each treated with amoxicillin. He denies ear pain, hearing difficulty, and breathing difficulty. Examination showed 3+ symmetric tonsils with cryptic debris and no exudate, tender anterior cervical lymph nodes, clear tympanic membranes, and normal visual acuity. The impression is recurrent tonsillitis with tonsillar hypertrophy, and tonsillectomy was discussed with his mother. The plan is referral for tonsillectomy, ibuprofen as needed, and a clinic visit in 4 weeks.

No known drug allergies and no daily medications.

Tender anterior cervical lymph nodes of about 1 cm palpable bilaterally. Tympanic membranes clear. Visual acuity 20/20 in each eye with no conjunctival injection or discharge.
soap.assessment: Recurrent tonsillitis with tonsillar hypertrophy; five documented episodes in one year meets criteria for surgical evaluation.
plan: Refer for tonsillectomy after discussing risks and benefits with his mother, who wishes to proceed
Ibuprofen 200 mg every 6 hours as needed for throat pain until surgery
Return to clinic in 4 weeks before the operation
Mother to call sooner for high fever or trouble swallowing

Hospital day 3 for a 63-year-old female admitted with sepsis from a urinary source due to E. coli pyelonephritis. Overnight she had no fever, rigors, or hypotension. This morning she reports that her flank pain and dysuria have improved, and she is tolerating a regular diet. She denies nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. She has no chest pain or shortness of breath. She has current tobacco use of about half a pack of cigarettes per day and asked about help quitting.

Current medications are ceftriaxone 1 g IV every 24 hours since admission, acetaminophen 650 mg every 6 hours as needed, and enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneously daily for VTE prophylaxis. IV fluids were stopped yesterday after her blood pressure normalized.

Vitals this morning: temperature 99.1 F, HR 88, BP 124/72, RR 16, SpO2 97% on room air. On exam she is comfortable and alert, mucous membranes are moist, and there is mild right CVA tenderness that is improved from admission. Abdomen is soft and non-tender, lungs are clear to auscultation, and there is no leg edema.

Data: WBC 11.2, down from 19.6 on admission. Creatinine 1.0, improved from 1.6 on admission. Admission blood cultures grew E. coli, and repeat blood cultures show no growth at 48 hours. Urine culture grew E. coli susceptible to ciprofloxacin and ceftriaxone. CT of the abdomen and pelvis on admission showed no obstructing stone or abscess.

Assessment and plan by problem. Sepsis from a urinary source due to E. coli pyelonephritis, clinically improving and hemodynamically stable. I am stopping IV ceftriaxone and starting ciprofloxacin 500 mg PO BID to complete 10 days of total therapy. AKI, resolved with fluids; continue to avoid NSAIDs and repeat a BMP in the morning. Current tobacco use: I counseled her on cessation and am starting a nicotine patch 14 mg daily. If she remains afebrile with a stable creatinine, she can likely be discharged tomorrow with primary care follow-up in 1 week.
summary: A 63-year-old female on hospital day 3 is being treated for sepsis from a urinary source due to Escherichia coli pyelonephritis. Her flank pain and dysuria have improved, she had no overnight fever, and her WBC and creatinine are trending down with stable vital signs. Admission blood cultures and the urine culture grew the organism, which is susceptible to ciprofloxacin and ceftriaxone. The plan is to switch IV ceftriaxone to oral ciprofloxacin to complete 10 days, repeat a BMP, avoid NSAIDs, and start a nicotine patch for current tobacco use, with possible discharge tomorrow.

Current medications ceftriaxone, acetaminophen as needed, and enoxaparin for VTE prophylaxis; IV fluids stopped yesterday.
soap.objective: Temperature 99.1 F, HR 88, BP 124/72, RR 16, SpO2 97% on room air. Comfortable and alert, mucous membranes moist, mild right CVA tenderness improved from admission, abdomen soft and non-tender, lungs clear, no leg edema. WBC 11.2 (19.6 on admission), creatinine 1.0 (1.6 on admission). Admission blood cultures grew E. coli; repeat blood cultures no growth at 48 hours. Urine culture grew E. coli susceptible to ciprofloxacin and ceftriaxone. CT of the abdomen and pelvis on admission showed no obstructing stone or abscess.
soap.assessment: Sepsis from a urinary source due to E. coli pyelonephritis, clinically improving and hemodynamically stable. AKI resolved with fluids. Current tobacco use.
plan: Stop IV ceftriaxone and start ciprofloxacin 500 mg PO BID to complete 10 days of total therapy
Continue acetaminophen 650 mg every 6 hours as needed and enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneously daily
Avoid NSAIDs and repeat a BMP in the morning
Cessation counseling and start nicotine patch 14 mg daily
Likely discharge tomorrow if afebrile with stable creatinine, with primary care follow-up in 1 week

A 65-year-old male is seen in the family medicine clinic with 10 days of nasal congestion and facial pressure. He first thought it was a cold and felt a little better around day 5, but then he got worse again with thick yellow-green nasal drainage, pain over both cheeks, and pain in his upper teeth. He also has a mild headache and a cough that is worse when he lies down. He denies fever, chills, vision changes, double vision, facial swelling, and neck stiffness.

He has hypertension and type 2 diabetes. When I asked him to tell me about his medicines, he could not read the names on the bottles and described a white pill and a small pink pill that he takes in the morning. He admits he sometimes skips them when he feels well. His daughter fills his pillbox on Sundays. From the pharmacy list that I reviewed with him, he takes lisinopril 20 mg daily and metformin 500 mg twice daily. He has no known drug allergies. Because of his limited health literacy, I used plain language and short sentences throughout the visit.

Vitals today: BP 138/82, HR 78, temperature 98.6 F, RR 16, SpO2 97% on room air. His fingerstick glucose was 156. His A1c was 7.4% at the last visit 2 months ago. On exam he has boggy nasal turbinates with thick yellow nasal drainage. Maxillary sinus tenderness is present bilaterally. The throat is mildly red without exudate, the tympanic membranes are normal, and the lungs are clear. There is no periorbital swelling.

My impression is acute bacterial sinusitis, since his symptoms have lasted more than 10 days and worsened after initial improvement. His hypertension and type 2 diabetes are reasonably controlled. I am starting amoxicillin-clavulanate 875 mg/125 mg twice daily with food for 7 days, saline nasal rinses twice daily, and fluticasone nasal spray 2 sprays in each nostril once daily. He may take acetaminophen 650 mg every 6 hours as needed for pain. I advised him to avoid pseudoephedrine decongestants because of his blood pressure. He will continue lisinopril and metformin. I asked him to repeat the instructions back to me, gave him a one-page medication schedule with pictures and large print, and our nurse will call him in 3 days to check on him. He should return sooner for vision changes, facial swelling, severe headache, or fever, and we will see him again in 2 weeks.
summary: A 65-year-old male with hypertension and type 2 diabetes presented with 10 days of nasal congestion, facial pressure, and thick yellow-green nasal drainage that worsened after initial improvement. He denies fever, chills, vision changes, and facial swelling, and exam showed bilateral maxillary sinus tenderness without periorbital swelling. He has limited health literacy and cannot read his medication labels. The impression is acute bacterial sinusitis with reasonably controlled chronic conditions. He was started on amoxicillin-clavulanate, saline rinses, and fluticasone nasal spray, with teach-back, a picture-based medication schedule, a nurse call in 3 days, and follow-up in 2 weeks.

soap.subjective: 65-year-old male with 10 days of nasal congestion and facial pressure, initial mild improvement around day 5 followed by worsening with thick yellow-green nasal drainage, pain over both cheeks, pain in the upper teeth, mild headache, and a cough worse when lying down. History of hypertension and type 2 diabetes; takes lisinopril 20 mg daily and metformin 500 mg twice daily, cannot read medication labels, sometimes skips pills when he feels well. No known drug allergies. Limited health literacy.
soap.objective: BP 138/82, HR 78, temperature 98.6 F, RR 16, SpO2 97% on room air. Fingerstick glucose 156; A1c 7.4% two months ago. Boggy nasal turbinates with thick yellow nasal drainage, bilateral maxillary sinus tenderness, throat mildly red without exudate, tympanic membranes normal, lungs clear, no periorbital swelling.
soap.assessment: Acute bacterial sinusitis (symptoms more than 10 days with worsening after initial improvement). Hypertension and type 2 diabetes reasonably controlled. Limited health literacy.
plan: Start amoxicillin-clavulanate 875 mg/125 mg twice daily with food for 7 days
Saline nasal rinses twice daily
Start fluticasone nasal spray 2 sprays in each nostril once daily
Acetaminophen 650 mg every 6 hours as needed for pain
Avoid pseudoephedrine decongestants because of hypertension
Continue lisinopril and metformin
Teach-back of instructions, one-page picture medication schedule in large print, nurse call in 3 days
Return sooner for vision changes, facial swelling, severe headache, or fever; follow up in 2 weeks

Doctor: Good afternoon. I see you're a 70-year-old male here for a follow-up on a kidney stone. How are you feeling?
Patient: Much better, doctor. I passed the stone three days ago. It came out in the strainer, a tiny gray speck, and I brought it in this little bag.
Doctor: Good, thank you for bringing it. And the pain that sent you to the emergency room last week, how is that?
Patient: Mostly gone. I just have a mild soreness on my right side, nothing like before.
Doctor: Any fever or chills?
Patient: No fever, no chills.
Doctor: Any blood in your urine now, or burning when you urinate?
Patient: The blood cleared up after the stone came out. No burning either.
Doctor: Any nausea or vomiting?
Patient: No, I'm eating fine.
Doctor: Are you still taking the tamsulosin and the ibuprofen they gave you?
Patient: I take the tamsulosin 0.4 mg every night. I took the ibuprofen 400 mg a few times, but not since the stone passed.
Doctor: Okay. Your blood pressure today is 132/80, heart rate 74, and temperature 98.3. Your belly is soft, and there's no tenderness over your back where the kidneys are. Your urinalysis today shows no blood and no signs of infection.
Patient: That's good to hear. Will I get another one?
Doctor: Stones can come back, so let's make that less likely. My impression is that you've passed your right ureteral stone and this episode has resolved. You can stop the tamsulosin now. We'll do a stone analysis so we know what it's made of, and I'd like a renal ultrasound in about four weeks to make sure there are no more stones. Drink enough water to make about two and a half liters of urine a day, and cut back on salt.
Patient: Okay, I can do that.
Doctor: Come back sooner if you have severe flank pain, fever, or blood in your urine.
Patient: Will do. Thank you.
summary: A 70-year-old male was seen in urgent care for follow-up of a kidney stone that he passed three days ago after an emergency room visit last week. He has only mild soreness on the right side and denies fever, chills, burning, nausea, and vomiting, and his blood in the urine has cleared. Vitals were normal, the abdomen was soft without tenderness over the kidneys, and the urinalysis showed no blood or infection. The impression is a passed right ureteral stone with the episode resolved. Tamsulosin was stopped, and a stone analysis, a renal ultrasound in four weeks, increased fluids, and less salt were advised.

soap.subjective: 70-year-old male following up after passing a kidney stone three days ago, which he brought in for analysis; he was seen in the emergency room last week with pain. Now has only mild soreness on the right side. Denies fever, chills, blood in the urine, burning, nausea, and vomiting. Taking tamsulosin 0.4 mg every night and took ibuprofen 400 mg a few times, none since the stone passed.
soap.objective: Blood pressure 132/80, heart rate 74, temperature 98.3. Abdomen soft, no tenderness over the kidneys. Urinalysis shows no blood and no signs of infection.
soap.assessment: Passed right ureteral stone; episode resolved.
plan: Stop tamsulosin
Stone analysis
Renal ultrasound in about four weeks to check for remaining stones
Drink enough water to make about two and a half liters of urine a day and cut back on salt
Return sooner for severe flank pain, fever, or blood in the urine

Doctor: Good afternoon. I understand you're a 56-year-old female with an itchy rash that's been getting worse. Tell me what's going on.
Patient: Hi, doctor. Yes. It started about three weeks ago on the insides of my elbows and the backs of my knees, and now it's on my hands and neck too. It itches so badly at night that I can't sleep. Is this contagious? I've been so worried about my husband and my grandkids.
Doctor: No, it isn't contagious. Have you had anything like this before?
Patient: I had eczema as a kid, but it went away. Is it back because of stress? I've been very stressed lately. Could it be something I'm eating?
Doctor: Stress can definitely make eczema flare. Any fever, or any areas that are oozing or crusting?
Patient: No fever, and nothing is oozing. A few spots on my fingers are cracked and they sting.
Doctor: Any new soaps, detergents, or lotions?
Patient: No, I've used the same fragrance-free soap for years. I do get hay fever in the spring, but no asthma.
Doctor: Okay. I see in your chart that you have hypertension, hypothyroidism, and high cholesterol. What medications and supplements are you taking?
Patient: Let me think. For my blood pressure, lisinopril 20 mg every morning. For my thyroid, levothyroxine, 125 micrograms every morning. Oh, wait, sorry, it's 75 micrograms. I just checked the pharmacy app. The 125 was my old dose before they lowered it. Then atorvastatin 20 mg at night. Over the counter, I take fish oil, turmeric capsules, and biotin 10,000 micrograms for my hair and nails. I've also been taking Benadryl 25 mg at bedtime for the itch, and cetirizine 10 mg once a day. And I've been putting hydrocortisone cream 1 percent on it twice a day, but it hasn't helped. Is any of that making it worse?
Doctor: That's very helpful, thank you. The lisinopril and the thyroid pill are not causing this. Your vitals today are blood pressure 138/84, heart rate 76, and temperature 98.4. On exam I see dry, scaly, thickened patches in both elbow creases and behind both knees, scratch marks, and fissures on the fingers. There are no honey-colored crusts, no pustules, and no weeping, so it doesn't look infected. I also looked at your last labs: TSH 2.1 and LDL 96, both fine.
Patient: So it's not cancer? And will the steroid cream thin my skin?
Doctor: It's not cancer. This is atopic dermatitis, a common eczema in adults. A stronger steroid for a short time is safe. I'm stopping the hydrocortisone 1 percent cream and starting triamcinolone 0.1 percent ointment twice daily for two weeks on the arms, legs, hands, and neck, but not on your face. I'm also stopping the Benadryl, since it can cause grogginess. Let's increase the cetirizine to 10 mg twice daily instead. Please stop the biotin and the turmeric. Biotin can throw off thyroid lab results, so I'll ask your primary doctor to repeat the TSH a few weeks after you stop it. The fish oil is fine to continue, along with your lisinopril, levothyroxine 75 micrograms, and atorvastatin.
Patient: What about moisturizer? And what if it doesn't get better?
Doctor: Use a thick fragrance-free moisturizer twice a day and right after short, lukewarm showers. If it isn't clearly better in two weeks, come back to the dermatology clinic and we'll discuss other options.
Patient: Okay. Should I call if it gets worse?
Doctor: Yes, call right away for fever, pus, or spreading redness.
summary: A 56-year-old female with hypertension, hypothyroidism, and high cholesterol presented to urgent care with a three-week itchy rash on the elbow creases, backs of the knees, hands, and neck that disrupts her sleep. She denies fever and oozing, and exam showed dry, scaly, thickened patches with scratch marks and finger fissures but no signs of infection. She clarified her levothyroxine dose as 75 micrograms and reported using several supplements; recent TSH was 2.1 and LDL 96. The diagnosis is atopic dermatitis. Hydrocortisone cream, Benadryl, biotin, and turmeric were stopped, triamcinolone ointment was started, and cetirizine was increased, with dermatology follow-up in two weeks.

soap.subjective: 56-year-old female, anxious with many questions, with an itchy rash for three weeks on the insides of the elbows and backs of the knees, now also on the hands and neck, itching badly at night. Had eczema as a child. Denies fever and oozing; fingers are cracked and sting. No new soaps, detergents, or lotions; hay fever in spring, no asthma. Medications: lisinopril 20 mg every morning, levothyroxine 75 micrograms every morning (first stated 125 micrograms, corrected after checking the pharmacy app), atorvastatin 20 mg at night, cetirizine 10 mg once a day, Benadryl 25 mg at bedtime, hydrocortisone cream 1 percent twice a day, and over-the-counter fish oil, turmeric capsules, and biotin 10,000 micrograms. History of hypertension, hypothyroidism, and high cholesterol.
soap.objective: Blood pressure 138/84, heart rate 76, temperature 98.4. Dry, scaly, thickened patches in both elbow creases and behind both knees, scratch marks, and fissures on the fingers; no honey-colored crusts, pustules, or weeping, so no sign of infection. Last labs: TSH 2.1 and LDL 96.
soap.assessment: Adult atopic dermatitis flare. Hypertension, hypothyroidism, and high cholesterol, on treatment.
plan: Stop hydrocortisone 1 percent cream
Start triamcinolone 0.1 percent ointment twice daily for two weeks on the arms, legs, hands, and neck, not on the face
Stop Benadryl and increase cetirizine to 10 mg twice daily
Stop biotin and turmeric; continue fish oil
Ask the primary doctor to repeat the TSH a few weeks after stopping biotin
Continue lisinopril, levothyroxine 75 micrograms, and atorvastatin
Thick fragrance-free moisturizer twice a day and after short lukewarm showers
Return to the dermatology clinic in two weeks if not clearly better; call right away for fever, pus, or spreading redness

note:
Dermatology clinic dictation on an 81-year-old female seen for a flare of adult atopic dermatitis. She has had itchy dry patches on the forearms, lower legs, and trunk for six weeks, correction, eight weeks, and the itching wakes her at night. She has a long history of eczema that was quiet for years until this winter. She denies fever, denies oozing or crusting, denies new soaps or detergents, and denies any new medications. Past history includes hypertension, for which she takes amlodipine 5 mg daily. She also takes hydroxyzine 25 mg at bedtime, started by her primary care provider for the itch, and she says it makes her groggy and unsteady in the morning. Social history is significant for heavy alcohol use, about four to five whiskey drinks every evening for many years. She denies morning shakes and denies any past withdrawal seizures.

Vitals are blood pressure 148/82, pulse 72, temperature 97.9, respiratory rate 16. On examination there are dry, scaly, lichenified plaques on both forearms and shins with linear excoriations. There is no weeping, no honey crusts, and no pustules. The face and neck are spared. There is mild dryness of the eyelids. The skin is diffusely xerotic. There is no lymphadenopathy.

Labs from her primary care provider last week show AST 64, ALT 41, platelets 148, MCV 101, and creatinine 0.9. Her AUDIT-C score today is 9.

Assessment, one, adult atopic dermatitis flare with xerosis. Two, heavy alcohol use with a mildly elevated AST and macrocytosis. Three, hypertension, stable. Plan, stop the hydroxyzine because of sedation and fall risk, especially in combination with alcohol. Start triamcinolone 0.1% ointment twice daily to the forearms, shins, and trunk for 2 weeks, then stop and reassess. Start hydrocortisone 2.5% ointment twice daily to the eyelids for up to 1 week. Thick petrolatum emollient twice daily and within three minutes of bathing. Start thiamine 100 mg daily. Continue amlodipine 5 mg daily. I counseled her about cutting down on alcohol, she is willing to try, and I will ask her primary care provider to follow the liver enzymes and discuss treatment options. Return to clinic in 3 weeks.
summary: An 81-year-old female with hypertension presented to dermatology with an eight-week flare of itchy dry patches on the forearms, lower legs, and trunk that wakes her at night. She has heavy alcohol use of about four to five whiskey drinks each evening and takes hydroxyzine at bedtime, which leaves her groggy and unsteady. Examination showed dry, scaly, lichenified plaques with excoriations and diffuse xerosis, and labs showed AST 64 and MCV 101. The assessment is an adult atopic dermatitis flare with xerosis, heavy alcohol use, and stable hypertension. Hydroxyzine was stopped, triamcinolone, hydrocortisone, and thiamine were started, alcohol reduction was counseled, and follow-up is in 3 weeks.

soap.subjective: 81-year-old female with a flare of adult atopic dermatitis: itchy dry patches on the forearms, lower legs, and trunk for eight weeks, with itching that wakes her at night, on a background of long-standing eczema. Denies fever, oozing or crusting, new soaps or detergents, and new medications. Hypertension on amlodipine 5 mg daily. Takes hydroxyzine 25 mg at bedtime from her primary care provider, which makes her groggy and unsteady in the morning. Heavy alcohol use, about four to five whiskey drinks every evening for many years; denies morning shakes and past withdrawal seizures.
soap.objective: Blood pressure 148/82, pulse 72, temperature 97.9, respiratory rate 16. Dry, scaly, lichenified plaques on both forearms and shins with linear excoriations; no weeping, honey crusts, or pustules. Face and neck spared, mild dryness of the eyelids, diffuse xerosis, no lymphadenopathy. AST 64, ALT 41, platelets 148, MCV 101, creatinine 0.9. AUDIT-C score 9.
soap.assessment: Adult atopic dermatitis flare with xerosis. Heavy alcohol use with mildly elevated AST and macrocytosis. Hypertension, stable.
plan: Stop hydroxyzine because of sedation and fall risk, especially with alcohol
Start triamcinolone 0.1% ointment twice daily to the forearms, shins, and trunk for 2 weeks, then stop and reassess
Start hydrocortisone 2.5% ointment twice daily to the eyelids for up to 1 week
Thick petrolatum emollient twice daily and within three minutes of bathing
Start thiamine 100 mg daily
Continue amlodipine 5 mg daily
Alcohol reduction counseling; ask the primary care provider to follow the liver enzymes and discuss treatment options
Return to clinic in 3 weeks

note:
Doctor: Good morning. You're a 43-year-old female here for a follow-up on the left wrist fracture from two weeks ago, correct?
Patient: Yes. I fell off my bike and broke my wrist.
Doctor: How is the pain?
Patient: Better. About a three out of ten most of the time. It throbs at night when my hand hangs down.
Doctor: Any numbness or tingling in your fingers?
Patient: No numbness, no tingling.
Doctor: Any increasing swelling, or fingers turning pale or blue?
Patient: The bruising is yellow now and spreads down into my hand, but my fingers are pink and warm. The swelling is no worse.
Doctor: That bruising is expected, especially since you're on a blood thinner. Remind me what you take?
Patient: Apixaban 5 mg twice a day for the clot in my lung I had last year. And I've been taking ibuprofen 400 mg for the wrist pain, about twice a day.
Doctor: Any nosebleeds, bleeding gums, or blood in your urine or stool?
Patient: No, nothing like that.
Doctor: Good. Ibuprofen together with apixaban raises your bleeding risk, so I want you to stop the ibuprofen. Use acetaminophen 650 mg every 6 hours as needed instead, and please don't stop the apixaban, because you still need it for your pulmonary embolism.
Patient: Okay. Should I take anything for bone healing?
Doctor: Vitamin D3 1,000 units daily is reasonable, along with calcium in your diet. Now, your blood pressure today is 118/74 and heart rate 70. The skin is intact, the bruising is over the forearm and into the hand, your capillary refill is under two seconds, and sensation and finger movement are normal. The X-ray of the wrist today shows the distal radius fracture is still in good alignment, with no loss of position.
Patient: So I don't need surgery?
Doctor: No surgery is needed. I'm going to take off the splint and put on a short-arm cast for four more weeks. We'll repeat the X-ray in two weeks, and after the cast comes off I'll send you to hand therapy. Keep the cast dry, and call us right away for increasing swelling, numbness, cold or blue fingers, severe pain, or any unusual bleeding.
Patient: Will do. Thank you.
summary: A 43-year-old female on apixaban for a prior pulmonary embolism returned for follow-up of a left distal radius fracture from a bike fall two weeks ago. Her pain is about 3 out of 10 with expected bruising into the hand, and she denies numbness, tingling, and bleeding. Vitals were normal, neurovascular status was intact, and the wrist X-ray showed good alignment without loss of position. Ibuprofen was stopped because of the bleeding risk with apixaban, and acetaminophen and vitamin D3 were started. She will be placed in a short-arm cast for four more weeks with a repeat X-ray in two weeks and later hand therapy.

soap.subjective: 43-year-old female following up on a left wrist fracture from a bike fall two weeks ago. Start vitamin D3 1,000 units daily with dietary calcium

Repeat X-ray in two weeks
Hand therapy referral after the cast comes off

Hospital day 2 for a 74-year-old female admitted with acute bacterial sinusitis. She presented with 11 days of right facial pain, thick green nasal drainage, and a fever that returned after initial improvement, and she was admitted because of severe headache and poor oral intake. She is very anxious this morning and had many questions. She asked whether the infection could spread to her brain or eyes, whether she will need surgery, whether she caught it from a visitor, and why she is not getting an MRI. I answered each question in turn and reviewed the CT result with her, and she said she felt calmer afterward. Her facial pressure and headache are better today and she is drinking well. She denies vision changes, double vision, neck stiffness, confusion, and swelling around the eyes. She denies chest pain and shortness of breath.

Her history includes hypertension and type 2 diabetes. Current medications are ampicillin-sulbactam 3 g IV every 6 hours since admission, amlodipine 5 mg daily, and acetaminophen 650 mg every 6 hours as needed for headache. Metformin 500 mg BID was held on admission. She has no known drug allergies.

Vitals this morning: T 99.0 F, HR 82, BP 134/78, RR 16, SpO2 98% on room air. She appears anxious but is alert and oriented. She has right maxillary tenderness, purulent drainage in the right middle meatus, and boggy turbinates. There is no periorbital edema, extraocular movements are intact, and her neck is supple. Lungs are clear. Labs show WBC 12.4, down from 15.8 on admission, and creatinine 0.9. Fingerstick glucose has been 140 to 170. CT of the sinuses without contrast on admission showed an air-fluid level in the right maxillary sinus with mucosal thickening and no orbital or intracranial extension.

Impression is acute bacterial sinusitis, improving, with no complications on CT. Hypertension is controlled and type 2 diabetes is stable now that she is eating. Because she is tolerating a diet and improving, I am stopping IV ampicillin-sulbactam and starting amoxicillin-clavulanate 875 mg/125 mg PO BID to finish 10 days of total therapy. I am also restarting metformin 500 mg BID with meals. We will continue amlodipine, add saline nasal irrigation twice daily, and continue acetaminophen as needed. I will refer her to ENT if symptoms do not continue to improve. She can likely go home tomorrow if she remains stable, and I will see her in clinic in 1 week.
summary: A 74-year-old female on hospital day 2 is being treated for acute bacterial sinusitis with hypertension and type 2 diabetes. She was anxious and asked many questions about complications, and her facial pressure and headache are improving; she denies vision changes, double vision, neck stiffness, and confusion. Exam showed right maxillary tenderness and purulent drainage without periorbital edema, her WBC fell to 12.4, and CT showed a right maxillary air-fluid level without orbital or intracranial extension. IV ampicillin-sulbactam was changed to oral amoxicillin-clavulanate and metformin was restarted. Discharge is likely tomorrow with clinic follow-up in 1 week.

84-year-old female seen in geriatrics clinic for advance care planning and follow-up of her chronic conditions, which include heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, stage 3 chronic kidney disease, and osteoarthritis of both knees. She came with her daughter. She no longer drives and depends on her daughter, who works full-time, for rides. The clinic is about 40 minutes from her home, and she missed her last two visits because no ride was available. Her daughter is worried that follow-up will keep slipping.

She feels stable overall. She has knee pain that is worse with walking and takes over-the-counter naproxen 220 mg twice daily for it. She denies chest pain, orthopnea, leg swelling, lightheadedness when she stands, and falls in the past year. She also denies low mood. She takes furosemide 20 mg daily and lisinopril 5 mg daily.

Vitals: BP 128/70, HR 68, SpO2 96% on room air, weight 61 kg, unchanged from the last visit. On exam both knees have crepitus with mild bony enlargement. The lungs are clear, and there is no jugular venous distension, peripheral edema, or knee effusion. Labs from 2 weeks ago showed creatinine 1.3 with eGFR 38 and potassium 4.4.

We spent most of the visit on advance care planning. She understands her heart and kidney conditions and has decision-making capacity. She wants to stay in her own home as long as possible. She would not want CPR or a breathing machine if her heart stopped, but she would accept hospital treatment for reversible problems. She named her daughter as her health care surrogate, and her daughter agreed. We completed a health care surrogate designation and a POLST form with a DNR/DNI order today, and copies were given to both of them and scanned into the chart.

Impression: advance care planning completed, heart failure with preserved ejection fraction compensated, stage 3 chronic kidney disease stable, and knee osteoarthritis. I am stopping naproxen because of her kidney disease and heart failure and starting acetaminophen 650 mg three times daily. We will continue furosemide 20 mg daily and lisinopril 5 mg daily. Because of her transportation barriers, I placed a referral to social work for paratransit enrollment and ride assistance, and I arranged home health nursing visits. A BMP will be drawn at a lab near her home in 2 weeks. Her next visit in 3 months will be by video, and she will call sooner for weight gain, swelling, or shortness of breath.

Transportation barriers have caused her to miss recent visits. She denies chest pain, orthopnea, leg swelling, and falls, and she has capacity and chose a DNR/DNI order with her daughter as health care surrogate. Naproxen was stopped because of her kidney disease and heart failure and acetaminophen was started, with social work, home health nursing, a BMP in 2 weeks, and a video visit in 3 months.

Doctor: Good morning. I'm using a professional interpreter on the video line so we can speak in your language. You're an 84-year-old male here for your routine HIV follow-up, and we're seeing you in urgent care today because the clinic had no openings. Is that right?
Patient: Yes, doctor. I have been well. I take my HIV pill every day.
Doctor: Do you ever miss a dose?
Patient: Maybe one time in the last three months, when I was traveling to see my son.
Doctor: Which pill do you take?
Patient: Biktarvy, one tablet once a day, in the morning.
Doctor: Any fever, night sweats, or weight loss?
Patient: No fever, no night sweats, and my weight is the same.
Doctor: Any diarrhea or nausea with the medicine?
Patient: No diarrhea, no nausea.
Doctor: Any cough, shortness of breath, or chest pain?
Patient: No, nothing like that. Sometimes I get a headache in the evening, and my neighbor said my blood pressure is high.
Doctor: Let me check. Your blood pressure today is 158/90, and it was 154/88 at your last two visits. Heart rate is 72 and temperature is 98.2. Your heart and lungs sound normal. I don't see any swelling in your legs, mouth sores, or rashes, and your lymph nodes are not enlarged.
Patient: What about my blood tests?
Doctor: Your labs from last week show an HIV viral load that is undetectable, and your CD4 count is 540. Your creatinine is 1.0, and your cholesterol is acceptable on the atorvastatin. Are you still taking atorvastatin 20 mg at bedtime?
Patient: Yes, every night.
Doctor: Any other medicines, vitamins, or antacids?
Patient: Only calcium tablets sometimes, for my stomach.
Doctor: Calcium can lower how much of the HIV medicine your body absorbs, so please don't take the calcium tablets within two hours of your Biktarvy.
Patient: Okay, I will take them in the evening.
Doctor: My impression is that your HIV is well controlled on Biktarvy, but your high blood pressure is not controlled. I'm starting amlodipine 5 mg once a day. Keep taking Biktarvy and atorvastatin the same way. I'll order a basic metabolic panel in 2 weeks, and we'll repeat the HIV viral load and CD4 count in 6 months. Come back in 4 weeks to recheck your blood pressure, and go to the emergency room for a severe headache, chest pain, or vision changes.
Patient: I understand. Thank you for the interpreter.
summary: An 84-year-old male was seen in urgent care with a professional interpreter for routine HIV follow-up on Biktarvy, reporting good adherence with one missed dose in three months. He denies fever, night sweats, weight loss, diarrhea, nausea, cough, shortness of breath, and chest pain, though he has an occasional evening headache. Blood pressure was elevated at 158/90 and the HIV viral load was undetectable with a CD4 count of 540. The impression is well-controlled HIV with uncontrolled high blood pressure. Amlodipine was started, calcium tablets were separated from Biktarvy by two hours, and a basic metabolic panel in 2 weeks and a blood pressure recheck in 4 weeks were arranged.

soap.assessment: HIV well controlled on Biktarvy. High blood pressure, not controlled.

Continue Biktarvy and atorvastatin unchanged
Do not take calcium tablets within two hours of Biktarvy

Repeat HIV viral load and CD4 count in 6 months
Return in 4 weeks to recheck blood pressure; go to the emergency room for severe headache, chest pain, or vision changes

A 75-year-old female was seen in the orthopedic specialty clinic for 4 months of numbness and tingling in the right hand. The symptoms involve the thumb, index, and middle fingers and are worst at night, waking her several times a week. Shaking her hand relieves them. She also notices that she occasionally drops her coffee cup. She denies neck pain, denies pain radiating up the arm, and denies any injury to the wrist. Her only chronic condition is hypothyroidism, treated with levothyroxine 75 micrograms daily.

On examination the right wrist has no swelling or deformity. Tinel sign and Phalen test are positive on the right. Sensation is reduced to light touch in the thumb, index, and middle fingers. There is no thenar atrophy, and thumb abduction strength is 5/5. Cervical spine range of motion is full and Spurling test is negative.

My impression is right carpal tunnel syndrome, mild to moderate. I discussed the treatment options with her. She will wear a neutral wrist splint at night, and I am ordering nerve conduction studies of the right upper extremity to confirm the diagnosis and grade its severity. She will continue levothyroxine unchanged. If her symptoms persist after 6 weeks of splinting, we will consider a corticosteroid injection. She will follow up in 6 weeks, or sooner if she notices worsening weakness.
summary: A 75-year-old female with hypothyroidism was seen in orthopedics for 4 months of numbness and tingling in the right thumb, index, and middle fingers that is worse at night and relieved by shaking the hand. She denies neck pain, pain radiating up the arm, and wrist injury. Examination showed positive Tinel sign and Phalen test, reduced sensation in the median distribution, and no thenar atrophy. The impression is right carpal tunnel syndrome, mild to moderate. The plan is a neutral wrist splint at night, nerve conduction studies, unchanged levothyroxine, and follow-up in 6 weeks.

Doctor: Hello. I understand you're a 70-year-old female who had a seizure this morning. Can you tell me what happened?
Patient: Honestly, I don't remember much. I was making breakfast, and the next thing I knew I was on the kitchen floor.
Family member: I was in the kitchen with her. She stared blankly, then she fell to the floor and her whole body started jerking. It lasted about two minutes. Her lips looked blue, and she was confused for about 20 minutes afterward.
Doctor: Did she bite her tongue or lose control of her bladder?
Family member: She bit the side of her tongue, but she didn't wet herself.
Doctor: Have you ever had a seizure before?
Patient: No, never.
Doctor: Any head injury, fever, headache, or weakness on one side recently?
Patient: No head injury, no fever, no headache, no weakness. My vision is fine. I haven't had any alcohol, and I slept well last night.
Doctor: Any history of stroke? Any other medical conditions?
Patient: No stroke. I only have high blood pressure, and I take lisinopril 10 mg every morning.
Doctor: Your vitals are blood pressure 142/84, heart rate 78, temperature 98.4, and oxygen level 98 percent. Your fingerstick glucose is 112. On exam you're awake and alert, you're speaking normally, your cranial nerves are normal, strength and sensation are equal on both sides, and your walking is steady. There's a small bite mark on the left side of your tongue.
Patient: Is that good news?
Doctor: It's reassuring. My impression is a first unprovoked seizure. I'm not starting a seizure medicine today. I'm sending you to the emergency department now for a CT of your head and blood tests, and I'll arrange an MRI of the brain and an EEG as an outpatient. No driving until you've seen the neurologist, and avoid baths, heights, and swimming alone. Continue your lisinopril. You'll see neurology in one week, and call 911 if another seizure lasts more than five minutes.
Patient: Okay, thank you.
summary: A 70-year-old female with high blood pressure had her first seizure this morning, witnessed by a family member as a blank stare followed by whole-body jerking for about two minutes, a bitten tongue, and 20 minutes of confusion. She denies head injury, fever, headache, and weakness, and she did not wet herself. Vitals and fingerstick glucose were normal and the neurologic exam was normal apart from a small tongue bite. The impression is a first unprovoked seizure. No seizure medicine was started; she was sent to the emergency department for a head CT and blood tests, with an outpatient MRI, EEG, driving restriction, and neurology follow-up in one week.
